regimens.indication: Acute Seizure Episodes / Rapid Intravenous Replacement in Epilepsy

refs.quote: Valproate sodium injection is indicated as an intravenous alternative in patients in whom oral administration of valproate products is temporarily not feasible in the following conditions: • Monotherapy and adjunctive therapy of complex partial seizures and simple and complex absence seizures; adjunctive therapy in patients with multiple seizure types that include absence seizures ( 1 )

In one clinical safety study, approximately 90 patients with epilepsy and with no measurable plasma levels of valproate were given single infusions of valproate sodium injection (up to 15 mg/kg and mean dose of 1,184 mg) over 5 to 10 minutes (1.5 to 3 mg/kg/min). Patients generally tolerated the more rapid infusions well [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] .

regimens.dose_text: Single IV infusion up to 15 mg/kg (over 5 to 10 minutes at 1.5 to 3 mg/kg/min) or standard infusion over 60 minutes (rate not to exceed 20 mg/min). In status epilepticus protocols, guidelines endorse up to 30 to 40 mg/kg IV.

regimens.indication: Complex Partial Seizures and Absence Seizures (Maintenance IV Dosing)

refs.quote: Complex Partial Seizures in Adults and Children 10 years of age or older: Initial dose is 10 to 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day to achieve optimal clinical response. Maximum recommended dose is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 ).

Valproate sodium injection should be administered as a 60 minute infusion (but not more than 20 mg/min) with the same frequency as the oral products, although plasma concentration monitoring and dosage adjustments may be necessary.

regimens.dose_text: Initial maintenance dose 10 to 15 mg/kg/day administered in divided doses every 6 to 8 hours (each dose infused over 60 minutes, not exceeding 20 mg/min). Increase at 1-week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day to achieve optimal clinical response (usual therapeutic target 50 to 100 mcg/mL). Maximum recommended dose 60 mg/kg/day.

value: WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS: Hepatotoxicity, including fatalities, usually during the first 6 months of treatment. Children under two years of age and patients with mitochondrial disorders are at higher risk. Monitor patients closely and perform serum liver testing prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter. Fetal Risk: Major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects, and decreased IQ. Pancreatitis: Life-threatening pancreatitis including hemorrhagic cases.

Valproate sodium exists as the valproate ion in the blood. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).

mg_safety.note: Valproate does not impair neuromuscular transmission; considered a safe ASM in myasthenia gravis

ng_tube.note: Valproate sodium injection is for intravenous use; oral divalproex sodium sprinkle capsules or oral solution are preferred for enteral tube administration

value.clinical_action: Contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG; e.g. Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome) due to high risk of fatal hepatotoxicity.

value.effect: Clinically significant reduction in serum valproic acid concentrations (often by 60-90%), resulting in rapid loss of seizure control.
value.management: Avoid concomitant use. Alternative antibacterial or anticonvulsant therapy should be considered if carbapenems are required.

refs.quote: A clinically significant reduction in serum valproic acid concentration has been reported in patients receiving carbapenem antibiotics (for example, ertapenem, imipenem, meropenem this is not a complete list) and may result in loss of seizure control.

value.effect: Estrogen induces UGT glucuronidation, increasing valproate clearance and decreasing serum concentrations, risking breakthrough seizures.
value.management: Monitor serum valproate concentrations and clinical response when adding or discontinuing estrogen-containing contraceptives; dosage adjustments may be necessary.

refs.locator: Section 7.1 Effects of Co-Administered Drugs on Valproate Clearance
refs.quote: Estrogen-containing hormonal contraceptives may increase the clearance of valproate, which may result in decreased concentration of valproate and potentially increased seizure frequency.

value.effect: Aspirin displaces valproate from plasma protein binding sites (4-fold increase in free fraction) and inhibits valproate hepatic beta-oxidation.
value.management: Caution should be observed if valproate and aspirin are to be co-administered, especially in pediatric patients or when high aspirin doses are used.

refs.locator: Section 7.1 Effects of Co-Administered Drugs on Valproate Clearance
refs.quote: A study involving the co-administration of aspirin at antipyretic doses (11 to 16 mg/kg) with valproate to pediatric patients (n = 6) revealed a decrease in protein binding and an inhibition of metabolism of valproate. Valproate free fraction was increased 4-fold in the presence of aspirin compared to valproate alone.

value.effect: Rifampin increases oral clearance of valproate by ~40%, causing subtherapeutic valproate concentrations.
value.management: Valproate dosage adjustment and serum concentration monitoring are necessary when co-administered with rifampin.

refs.locator: Section 7.1 Effects of Co-Administered Drugs on Valproate Clearance
refs.quote: A study involving the administration of a single dose of valproate (7 mg/kg) 36 hours after 5 nights of daily dosing with rifampin (600 mg) revealed a 40% increase in the oral clearance of valproate. Valproate dosage adjustment may be necessary when it is co-administered with rifampin.

folic_acid.value: Folic acid supplementation prior to conception and during the first trimester is recommended, though it may not fully prevent valproate-induced malformations.

refs.quote: Evidence suggests that folic acid supplementation prior to conception and during the first trimester of pregnancy decreases the risk for congenital neural tube defects in the general population.

pregnancy_pk.value: Valproate clearance increases during pregnancy with lower total plasma concentrations; monitor unbound valproate concentrations.

Valproate is excreted in human milk. Data in the published literature describe the presence of valproate in human milk (range: 0.4 mcg/mL to 3.9 mcg/mL), corresponding to 1% to 10% of maternal serum levels.

lactation_summary.value: Valproate is excreted in human milk (1% to 10% of maternal serum levels). Monitor breastfed infants for somnolence, jaundice, or bruising.
